tier_reason: The libsimdxml README does show expat (SAX) and libxml2 (DOM) rows with exactly the claimed numbers, but it is a 0-star competitor's README: the harness (tmp/benchmark/orchestrator.sh) is not in the repository (404 on raw.githubusercontent.com, no tmp/ directory), the expat and libxml2 versions, compiler and flags are unstated, and the modes differ (SAX vs DOM). That is third-party numbers with partial methodology and no public code, so C, not A or B.

corrections.hardware: Intel Core i7-4850HQ (Haswell, 2013 laptop). The cross-language table (expat 15.495 ms vs libxml2 35.168 ms) ran at the 2.3 GHz base clock with no turbo; the wall/CPU/memory table (11.525 vs 26.507 ms, 121.381 vs 263.196 ms) is the 24.09.2026 run ab_quick_20260924_001320 at about 3.3 GHz (schedutil governor, turbo on, scaling_max_freq 3.5 GHz, load about 2.0 at start).
corrections.caveats: Weak and contested evidence. Expat's own README says only 'Fast streaming XML parser written in C99 with >90% test coverage', with no numbers. The figures come from the README of a competing 2026 project (KrzysztofKowalski/libsimdxml, 0 stars, 18 commits, a C++23 port of the Rust simdxml) that lists expat and libxml2 only as references. The harness is not public: the README's tmp/benchmark/orchestrator.sh and tools/rss_sampler.py are not in the repository. Expat and libxml2 versions, compiler and flags are not stated. The two libsimdxml tables were taken at different clocks (2.3 GHz base without turbo for the 15.495/35.168 ms cross-language table; about 3.3 GHz with turbo for the 11.525/26.507 and 121.381/263.196 ms wall/CPU/memory table), so ratios hold only within a table. The compared modes differ (Expat streaming SAX events vs libxml2 building a full DOM tree, which also explains the 25.44 vs 197.37 MiB peak RSS at 10 MB), so this is not like-for-like; the win belongs to streaming, not to the parser. Like-for-like data points the other way: bemayer/xml-benchmark (report/index.html committed, run dated 2026-04-06T17:17:26Z, runner 'local', hardware, compiler and versions not stated, Docker images with latest versions) has libxml2 SAX/Stream faster than Expat at every size: 1KB 0.028 vs 0.046 ms, 100KB 2.104 vs 10.178 ms, 1MB 39.606 vs 70.714 ms, 10MB 110.529 vs 145.468 ms, 100MB 592.34 vs 933.022 ms, and 104.826 vs 234.468 ms in a group labelled 'other' (that report's time and throughput columns imply input sizes other than the group labels, e.g. the '1MB' group works out to about 24 MB, so its labels are unreliable, but each within-group comparison favours libxml2). Search snippets of older posts (pages not opened, snippet only) disagree: a 2011 OSM-dev post has Expat about 10% faster than libxml2 on OSM data, a 2006 GNOME xml-list post has libxml2 about 30% faster on most test data, and an OpenOffice wiki page calls libxml2 SAX the fastest. Security: the libexpat repo shows a caution banner 'Expat has unfixed security issues' pointing to issue #1160 (open since 2026-03-06), which tracks about 30 non-public reports (DoS loops, NULL function-pointer dereferences, out-of-bounds access, UTF-16 surrogate validation).

notes: Record is accurate: the claimed numbers match the libsimdxml README rows exactly, and license MIT (expat/COPYING), 1.4k stars (555 forks), last commit 2026-10-06 and active status all check out. Shortcomings to record: not faster than libxml2 in a like-for-like SAX comparison (bemayer/xml-benchmark has libxml2 SAX ahead at all five sizes), the only win is Expat SAX vs libxml2 DOM from a 0-star competitor's README whose harness is not public, and the two quoted tables ran at different clocks (hardware corrected). Also record the open issue #1160 (about 30 unfixed non-public security reports).
